messages.subject: How to increase java heap size?
messages.subject_clean: How to increase java heap size?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

While using the xlsx package to read xlsx files, I get an error that
it has run out of java heap space.
However, I can't seem to find a way to increase the heap size.
I have found that this should do the trick:
options( java.parameters = "-Xmx1200m" )

Xlsx still crashes and didn't seem to take more memory.
Therefore, I tried to see what the maximum available amount of heap
space is in an instance.
By:
.jinit()
.jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "totalMemory")
.jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "maxMemory")

returning:
16318464
and:
259522560

I have also tried the following:
.jinit(parameters="-Xmx1200m")
.jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "totalMemory")
.jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "maxMemory")

Same result.

And I have just found:
system("java -Xms512m -Xmx1536m")
.jinit()
.jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "totalMemory")
.jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "maxMemory")

And that also yields the same result.

Of course, I might be doing the measurement wrong, however I tested it
on another machine and it gave other results...
Could someone please help me with a good way to get at the available
heap space, and how to increase it for RJava?

Kind regards,

Willem

messages.subject: Re: How to increase java heap size?
messages.subject_clean: How to increase java heap size?
messages.body_plain:
Willem,

what you used works just fine on my machine:

> library(rJava)
> options( java.parameters = "-Xmx1200m" )
> .jinit()
> .jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "totalMemory")
[1] 85000192
> .jcall(.jnew("java/lang/Runtime"), "J", "maxMemory")
[1] 1242562560

What really happens depends on your Java implementation - depending on the OS and Java it can refuse requests that are too big for your machine so it will revert to the default. So try clearing up some memory on your machine or lower your limit.  Note that on 32-bit systems you'll need contiguous memory of that size for the heap. You didn't say which OS you use but some of the less capable OSes like 32-bit Windows have hard time providing large contiguous memory to applications.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
马可,

can you, please, try NOT setting JAVA_HOME and PATH? Under normal circumstances you should NOT set them as they will override system settings (given that since 2.12.0 R is multi-arch you cannot set them globally as they will be wrong!). If that doesn't help, please do include the details on your OS. Finally, there is a chance that Java doesn't like your locale - check the locale used by JGR and Rgui respectively.

Cheers,
Simon

BTW: the message you reference has a completely different issue of .

I'm not quite sure I follow. My interpretation of your question is "what is the difference between RForge.net and R-Forge.R-project.org?". Answer to that is that some time back we started talking on R-core about some kind of infrastructure for packages authors, but for a while nothing happened. So I started my Rforge.net as a system written from scratch for the development of R packages, focused specifically on things that are unique to R (check on commit, automated binary builds, automated docs etc.). In the beginning I used it for my packages but then I made it public and other people joined as well. Not long thereafter some volunteers at the WU put up gforge-based site that was used to host R packages. The latter became the "official" R-Forge.R-project.org site with R-Fondation support.
  I kept my RForge.net because I don't think gforge is a good way to deal with packages, personally I think the UI is awful. I prefer a solution better tailored to R needs and those who feel the same use RForge.net. So the bottom line that both are trying to address the same problem just in different ways.

As for CRAN/BioC they have nothing to do with either RForge.net or the R-Forge. Often people submit their packages from the development system to CRAN as the release them, but those are independent. 

I hope that answers your questions somewhat. If that's not what you asked, please try to explain.

Cheers,
Simon

Not long thereafter some volunteers at the WU put up gforge-based site that was used to host R packages. The latter became the "official" R-Forge.R-project.org site with R-Fondation suppo
 rt. I kept my RForge.net because I don't think gforge is a good way to deal with packages, personally I think the UI is awful. I prefer a solution better tailored to R needs and those who feel the same use RForge.net. So the bottom line that both are trying to address the same problem just in different ways.
>> 
>> As for CRAN/BioC they have nothing to do with either RForge.net or the R-Forge. Often people submit their packages from the development system to CRAN as the release them, but those are independent.
>> 
>> I hope that answers your questions somewhat. If that's not what you asked, please try to explain.
> 
>> 
> From what I can see RForge.net looks nicer, and it seems to contain mostly software-development related packages. Also, it looks like there is one R package per project, unlike RForge.org where package collections targeted to a particular subject area can be maintained.
> 

Yes, RForge.net assumes one package per repository. However, that's something that could be changed if the need arises as we already have a way to produce multiple packages from one repository.


> Incidentally, I found your experimental threads package on RForge.net but haven't used it yet because
> it requires 2.13.0. I guess this means the new version of R will support thread-safe execution?

No :). That would be very nice, but the consensus is that it would require pretty much a re-write of R.

"threads" allows C code to be executed in parallel - i.e. packages can mark sections of their C code as thread-safe and those can be then executed in parallel across packages.  It is sort of a mix between "multicore" and threads support. It's experimental, though - that's why it's a package and not in core R ;).

The reason it requires R 2.13.0 is that I had to add a way for a function to obtain its current protection stack which was not there before.

Cheers,
Simon
